name: For Ujala Khush, Leadship Means Reliability not Recognition

content.title: For Ujala Khush, Leadship Means Reliability not Recognition
content.summary: AKU shaped Ujala into a nurse who leads through care, commitment, and accountability.

media.alt: For Ujala Khush, Leadship Means Reliability not Recognition

content.text: Ujala Khush was raised by a single mother whose quiet strength shaped her understanding of independence, resilience, and responsibility. Watching her mother navigate life with determination taught Ujala early that a woman must stand on her own-not just for herself, but for those who rely on her. This upbringing instilled purpose in Ujala, and from a young age, she stepped into academic and leadership roles, driven by curiosity, growth, and purpose.

At AKU, Ujala's definition of success began to evolve. Personal achievement remained important, but her time at AKU's School of Nursing and Midwifery taught her to look beyond herself and embrace her responsibility toward society. Nursing became more than a profession; it became a commitment to service grounded in empathy, accountability, and meaningful impact.

"I learned that leadership does not always mean being the loudest voice; it often means being the most reliable one," she says. "Nursing, to me, is not limited to bedside care; it is about improving systems, supporting people, and leading with integrity."

Falah has always been close to Ujala's heart. She joined in her second year, inspired by the idea that creativity, collaboration, and joy can be powerful tools to help those in need. In her final year, she led a team of over 160 members as Convener, organizing events and raising valuable funds for patients who otherwise may not have had access to care.

In clinical rotations, Ujala frequently served as a team lead, mentoring peers, supporting juniors, and ensuring smooth, safe care. Outside the hospital, she served her community as an active Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) member for over eight years.

Balancing academics, leadership, and clinical responsibilities challenged Ujala, but also helped her discover her true potential. Over time, AKU became more than a university; it became a training ground for values. Exposure to diverse perspectives reinforced respect and collaboration, while faculty continually challenged her to think critically, act professionally, and reflect deeply on her role - not just as a nurse, but as a leader committed to making a meaningful impact.
